questions.question: What determines whether an object is eligible for garbage collection?
options: How many references to it were ever created during the program's lifetime
Whether it is still reachable by following references starting from a root (global variables, active function scopes)
questions.explanation: Modern garbage collectors use reachability (mark-and-sweep) — an object with zero paths back to a root is collected, regardless of its past reference count.

questions.question: Why don't two objects that reference each other (a circular reference) necessarily cause a memory leak?
options: JavaScript engines special-case circular references and always ignore them
If nothing outside that circular pair still references either object, neither is reachable from a root, so both are still collected together
Circular references are a syntax error
Because they are both automatically converted to null
questions.explanation: Reachability-based garbage collection doesn't care if objects reference each other — what matters is whether a root can still reach them, directly or indirectly.

questions.question: What is the standard fix for a memory leak caused by an event listener that's never removed?
options: Pair every addEventListener with a matching removeEventListener once the listener is no longer needed
Wrap the listener in a Promise
Use var instead of let inside the handler
questions.explanation: An unremoved listener keeps its closure (and everything captured in it) alive indefinitely — the fix is always to tear it down when it's no longer needed, which is exactly what cleanup functions in useEffect or ngOnDestroy exist for.

questions.question: You're implementing a search-as-you-type input that calls an API. Which technique should you use to avoid firing a request on every keystroke?
options: Throttle, so it fires at a fixed interval
Debounce, so it fires only after the user pauses typing for a set delay
Neither — always call the API on every keystroke
questions.explanation: Debounce delays execution until the triggering event stops firing for a period, which is exactly the desired behavior for search-as-you-type.
